plain: The big muscle of the buttock. It is the main muscle for standing up from sitting and for climbing stairs — not for ordinary walking.
detail: From the posterior gluteal line of the ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament. Most fibres end in the iliotibial tract; the deeper lower fibres reach the gluteal tuberosity of the femur. Supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2).
clinical: The upper outer quadrant of the buttock is the safe zone for an intramuscular injection, chosen specifically to avoid the sciatic nerve. Weakness gives a characteristic backward lurch of the trunk when the affected leg takes weight.

plain: A fan-shaped muscle on the side of the hip. When you stand on one leg it stops the opposite side of the pelvis from dropping.
detail: From the outer surface of the ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines to the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1).
clinical: Damage to the superior gluteal nerve produces a positive Trendelenburg sign: standing on the affected leg lets the opposite hip sag. Bilateral weakness gives a waddling gait.

plain: The smallest and deepest of the three buttock muscles, lying under gluteus medius and working with it.
detail: From the ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines to the anterior surface of the greater trochanter. Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.
clinical: Abducts and medially rotates the hip alongside gluteus medius; both are needed to keep the pelvis level in single-leg stance.

plain: A fan-shaped muscle filling the inside of the pelvic bone. With psoas it forms the main muscle that lifts the thigh.
detail: From the upper two-thirds of the iliac fossa, joining the tendon of psoas major to insert on the lesser trochanter of the femur. Supplied directly by the femoral nerve (L2, L3).
clinical: Iliacus and psoas together are the iliopsoas — the most powerful hip flexor. A psoas abscess can track down within the sheath and point below the inguinal ligament.

plain: A long thick muscle running from the lumbar spine, through the pelvis, to the top of the thigh bone. It is the deepest muscle of the back wall of the abdomen.
detail: From the transverse processes, bodies and intervertebral discs of T12 to L5, passing under the inguinal ligament to the lesser trochanter. Supplied by the anterior rami of L1 to L3.
clinical: Because it crosses in front of the hip, irritation from appendicitis or a psoas abscess causes pain on passive extension of the hip — the psoas sign. The lumbar plexus is formed within its substance.

plain: A pear-shaped muscle deep in the buttock, running out of the pelvis to the hip. It is the key landmark of the gluteal region.
detail: From the front of the sacrum, passing through the greater sciatic foramen to the upper border of the greater trochanter. Supplied by branches of L5, S1 and S2.
clinical: Everything else in the gluteal region is described as above or below piriformis. The sciatic nerve usually emerges below it; in some people it pierces the muscle, which is one explanation offered for piriformis syndrome.

meshNames: Tensor fasciae latae origin and insertion.r
plain: A short muscle at the front of the hip that tightens the fibrous band running down the outside of the thigh.
detail: From the anterior superior iliac spine and outer lip of the iliac crest into the iliotibial tract. Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.
clinical: By tightening the iliotibial tract it helps steady the extended knee — useful in quadriceps weakness, where patients learn to lock the knee this way.

plain: The most visible of the muscles that pull the thigh inwards, forming the inner border of the front of the thigh.
detail: From the body of the pubis below the pubic crest to the middle third of the linea aspera. Supplied by the obturator nerve (L2–L4).
clinical: Its palpable upper border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle. Its tendinous origin is a frequent site of groin strain in footballers.

plain: The largest muscle of the inner thigh. It is really two muscles in one, with two different nerve supplies.
detail: An adductor part from the ischiopubic ramus to the linea aspera, supplied by the obturator nerve; and a hamstring part from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle, supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.
clinical: The gap between its two parts is the adductor hiatus, through which the femoral vessels pass to become the popliteal vessels.

plain: The middle head of the quadriceps, running straight down the front of the thigh. It is the only one that crosses the hip as well as the knee.
detail: Straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine and reflected head from above the acetabulum, to the base of the patella and on to the tibial tuberosity. Supplied by the femoral nerve.
clinical: Because it crosses two joints it both flexes the hip and extends the knee, and it cannot do both fully at once — knee extension is weaker when the hip is already flexed.

meshNames: Long head of biceps femoris origin and insertion.r
plain: The hamstring on the outer side of the back of the thigh. Its tendon is the cord you can feel on the outer side behind the knee.
detail: Long head from the ischial tuberosity, short head from the linea aspera, inserting together on the head of the fibula. The long head is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, the short head by the common fibular division.
clinical: Its two heads have different nerve supplies, so it is the one hamstring that can be partly spared in a sciatic lesion. Its tendon forms the upper lateral boundary of the popliteal fossa, with the common fibular nerve running along its medial border.

plain: A hamstring on the inner side of the back of the thigh, with a long cord-like tendon for its lower half.
detail: From the ischial tuberosity to the upper medial surface of the tibia as part of the pes anserinus. Supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.
clinical: Its long tendon is commonly harvested as a graft for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

plain: The deepest hamstring on the inner side, named for the broad membrane-like tendon at its upper end.
detail: From the ischial tuberosity to the posterior aspect of the medial tibial condyle, giving an expansion that forms the oblique popliteal ligament. Supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.
clinical: A Baker's cyst typically arises from the bursa between semimembranosus and the medial head of gastrocnemius, presenting as a swelling in the popliteal fossa.

meshNames: Lat. head of gastrocnemius origin and insertion.r
Med. head of gastrocnemius origin and insertion.r
plain: The two-headed muscle that gives the calf its shape. It points the foot down and also helps bend the knee.
detail: Medial and lateral heads from above the femoral condyles, joining soleus to form the calcaneal tendon. Supplied by the tibial nerve (S1, S2).
clinical: Because it crosses both knee and ankle, it cannot be fully stretched with the knee extended and the ankle dorsiflexed at once — the basis for distinguishing gastrocnemius from soleus tightness (Silfverskiöld test).

plain: A broad flat muscle lying under the calf muscle. It is the workhorse of standing and walking, and its pumping action pushes blood back up the leg.
detail: From the soleal line of the tibia and the head and upper shaft of the fibula, joining gastrocnemius in the calcaneal tendon. Supplied by the tibial nerve.
clinical: Known as the peripheral heart: contraction squeezes the deep veins and drives venous return. Immobility removes that pump, which is a major factor in deep vein thrombosis.

plain: The muscle on the front of the shin that lifts the foot upwards as you walk, so the toes clear the ground.
detail: From the lateral condyle and upper lateral surface of the tibia to the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal. Supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5).
clinical: The main dorsiflexor. Its paralysis, usually from a common fibular nerve injury, causes foot drop and the compensating high-stepping gait.

plain: A deep calf muscle whose tendon curls under the inner ankle to hold up the arch of the foot.
detail: From the interosseous membrane and adjacent tibia and fibula, passing behind the medial malleolus to the tuberosity of the navicular and adjacent tarsals. Supplied by the tibial nerve.
clinical: The main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch. Tibialis posterior dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired adult flat foot.

plain: The three-headed muscle on the back of the arm. It is the muscle that straightens the elbow.
detail: Long head from the infraglenoid tubercle, lateral and medial heads from the humerus above and below the radial groove, inserting on the olecranon. Supplied by the radial nerve (C6–C8).
clinical: Its branches leave the radial nerve above the radial groove, so a mid-shaft humeral fracture spares elbow extension while still causing wrist drop. The triceps jerk tests C7.

plain: A flat muscle lying underneath the biceps. It is the main workhorse of bending the elbow, whichever way the forearm is turned.
detail: From the lower half of the anterior humerus to the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna. Supplied mainly by the musculocutaneous nerve, with a small radial nerve contribution.
clinical: Because it inserts on the ulna, which cannot rotate, brachialis flexes the elbow equally well in pronation and supination — unlike biceps.

plain: A muscle wrapping around the top of the radius that turns the palm upwards.
detail: From the lateral epicondyle, radial collateral and anular ligaments and the supinator crest of the ulna, wrapping around the upper radius. Supplied by the deep branch of the radial nerve, which passes through it.
clinical: The deep branch of the radial nerve pierces supinator between its two heads at the arcade of Frohse — a common entrapment site producing posterior interosseous nerve palsy, with finger drop but no sensory loss.

meshNames: Pronator teres humeral head origin and insertion.r
Pronator teres ulnar head origin and insertion.r
plain: A muscle running diagonally across the upper forearm that turns the palm downwards.
detail: Humeral head from the medial epicondyle and ulnar head from the coronoid process, inserting on the middle of the lateral surface of the radius. Supplied by the median nerve.
clinical: The median nerve passes between its two heads, where it can be compressed — pronator teres syndrome, which unlike carpal tunnel syndrome also numbs the central palm.

meshNames: Flexor digitorum superficialis origin and insertion.r
plain: The muscle that bends the middle joints of the fingers. Its tendons split to let the deeper tendons pass through.
detail: From the medial epicondyle, coronoid process and radius, to the sides of the middle phalanges of the four fingers. Supplied by the median nerve.
clinical: Each tendon splits around the profundus tendon at the proximal phalanx — the chiasma tendinum. Tested by holding the other fingers straight and asking the patient to bend the tested finger.

meshNames: Flexor digitorum profundus origin and insertion.r
plain: The deep muscle that bends the fingertips. It is the only muscle that can bend the last joint of a finger.
detail: From the upper ulna and interosseous membrane to the bases of the distal phalanges. Split supply: the medial half by the ulnar nerve, the lateral half by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.
clinical: That split supply is why an anterior interosseous nerve lesion weakens the index finger's distal joint specifically, producing an abnormal pinch — the 'OK sign' cannot be made properly.

meshNames: Flexor carpi ulnaris origin and insertion.r
plain: A muscle along the little-finger side of the front of the forearm, bending the wrist towards that side.
detail: Humeral head from the medial epicondyle and ulnar head from the olecranon and posterior ulna, to the pisiform, hook of hamate and 5th metacarpal. Supplied by the ulnar nerve — the only forearm flexor it supplies apart from half of profundus.
clinical: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm by passing between its two heads, just behind the medial epicondyle, which is why the nerve is so exposed there.

plain: The strap muscle running straight up the front of the abdomen, crossed by tendinous bands — the 'six pack'.
detail: From the pubic crest and symphysis to the 5th, 6th and 7th costal cartilages and xiphoid process. Enclosed in the rectus sheath and crossed by three or more tendinous intersections. Supplied by the lower six thoracic nerves.
clinical: Below the arcuate line the posterior rectus sheath is absent, so the muscle lies directly on the transversalis fascia — an important level in abdominal surgery. Divarication of the recti is common after pregnancy.

meshNames: External abdominal oblique origin and insertion.r
plain: The outermost of the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall. Its fibres run downwards and forwards, like hands in pockets.
detail: From the outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs to the iliac crest, pubic tubercle and linea alba. Its lower border rolls under to form the inguinal ligament.
clinical: Its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal, and the gap in it above the pubic tubercle is the superficial inguinal ring.

meshNames: Internal abdominal oblique muscle origin and insertion.r
plain: The middle of the three flat abdominal muscles. Its fibres run at right angles to the outer layer, which is what makes the wall strong.
detail: From the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lateral inguinal ligament to the lower ribs and linea alba. Its lowest fibres arch over the spermatic cord.
clinical: With transversus abdominis it forms the conjoint tendon and the roof of the inguinal canal. Its lowest fibres continue as the cremaster muscle, which produces the cremasteric reflex.

meshNames: Transverse abdominal muscle origin and insertion.r
plain: The deepest of the flat abdominal muscles, with fibres running straight across like a corset.
detail: From the lower six costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lateral inguinal ligament to the linea alba and pubic crest. Supplied by the lower thoracic and first lumbar nerves.
clinical: The neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall lies between internal oblique and transversus abdominis — the target for a TAP block.

plain: The dome-shaped sheet separating the chest from the abdomen. It is the main muscle of breathing — when it flattens, air is drawn in.
detail: Sternal, costal and lumbar parts converging on a central tendon. Supplied by the phrenic nerves (C3, C4, C5). Three main openings: caval at T8, oesophageal at T10, aortic at T12.
clinical: Remember the openings as 'I ate ten eggs at twelve' — vena cava T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12. Irritation of the diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder tip, because both share the C3–C5 supply.

plain: The thick chewing muscle you can feel bulge at the angle of the jaw when you clench your teeth.
detail: From the zygomatic arch to the lateral surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible. Supplied by the masseteric branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3).
clinical: The most powerful muscle of mastication by cross-sectional area. All four muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

plain: A broad fan-shaped muscle on the side of the head that closes the jaw and pulls it backwards.
detail: From the temporal fossa, passing deep to the zygomatic arch to the coronoid process of the mandible. Supplied by deep temporal branches of CN V3.
clinical: Its posterior fibres retract the mandible, returning it after protrusion. Wasting of temporalis hollows the temple and is a visible sign of trigeminal motor loss.

plain: A short muscle deep in the cheek that pulls the jaw forwards — and it is the muscle that opens the mouth.
detail: Upper head from the greater wing of the sphenoid and lower head from the lateral pterygoid plate, inserting on the neck of the mandible and the capsule and disc of the temporomandibular joint.
clinical: The only muscle of mastication that opens the jaw; the other three close it. Its attachment to the articular disc means it is central to temporomandibular joint dysfunction and disc displacement.

meshNames: Medial pterygoid muscle origin and insertion.r
plain: A deep chewing muscle on the inner side of the jaw, mirroring masseter on the outside.
detail: From the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and the tuberosity of the maxilla to the medial surface of the angle of the mandible. Supplied by CN V3.
clinical: It slings the mandible with masseter on the outer surface. Injecting into it during an inferior alveolar nerve block causes trismus.

plain: The muscle of the cheek. It keeps food between the teeth while chewing and lets you blow out a candle.
detail: From the outer surfaces of the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible and the pterygomandibular raphe, to blend with orbicularis oris at the angle of the mouth. Supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
clinical: A muscle of facial expression, not of mastication — so it is supplied by the facial nerve, not the trigeminal. In facial palsy food collects in the affected cheek.

plain: The ring of muscle around the mouth that closes and purses the lips.
detail: A complex sphincter of fibres encircling the mouth, many derived from buccinator and other facial muscles. Supplied by the facial nerve.
clinical: Needed for whistling, sucking and articulating the letters p and b. Weakness in facial palsy causes drooling and slurred speech.

plain: A broad thin sheet of muscle just under the skin of the neck. It tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the corners of the mouth down.
detail: From the fascia over pectoralis major and deltoid, upwards across the clavicle to the lower border of the mandible and the skin of the lower face. Supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve.
clinical: It lies within the superficial fascia, so neck incisions are closed in a separate platysmal layer to give a good scar.

meshNames: Erector spinae muscles origin and insertion.r
plain: The long columns of muscle running either side of the spine. They straighten the back and hold you upright against gravity.
detail: Three columns from lateral to medial — iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis — arising from a broad tendon on the sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spines. Supplied segmentally by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves.
clinical: Remember the order laterally to medially as 'I Love Spine'. Being supplied by posterior rami is the defining feature of the true (intrinsic) back muscles.
